**2. FACILITY OVERVIEW**

GreenScape Tech Park (GSTP) is a multi-tenant commercial facility comprising four office blocks (Buildings A, B, C, and D), a central amenities building, two basement levels, and a surface parking area. The total built-up area is 185,000 square meters. The facility operates primarily from 08:00 to 20:00 on weekdays; however, the Data Centre (Building D) and certain critical labs operate 24x7.

The facility receives power from the BESCOM grid at two separate 11 kV feeders. Backup power is provided by four diesel generators (2 x 1250 kVA, 2 x 800 kVA). A 500 kWp rooftop solar PV installation was commissioned in March 2023 and is currently operational.

---

**3. METHODOLOGY**

The audit was conducted using a combination of:
- Review of BESCOM utility bills and monthly consumption logs (January 2023 – December 2023).
- On-site walkthrough inspections of all plant rooms, electrical rooms, and common areas.
- Power quality analysis and load profiling using Fluke 435 series analyzers on major feeders.
- Review of BMS (Building Management System) trends for HVAC equipment.
- Interviews with facility operators and maintenance staff.

All measurements were taken under normal operating conditions. Data loggers were deployed for a period of 14 days (January 15-28, 2023) to capture load profiles.

**5. PEAK DEMAND ANALYSIS**

**5.1 Peak Demand Overview**

The maximum demand recorded at the main incoming feeder (11 kV, BESCOM supply) during the
monitoring period was 4.8 MW. According to the Energy Audit Report 2023, GreenScape Tech Park's
peak_demand_2023 was 4.8 MW. This is the current and definitive peak demand value for the facility
for the calendar year 2023, and it has been cross-verified against the 33 kV metering data provided
by BESCOM as well as the internal power quality analyser logs. This value is used as the basis for
all demand-related calculations and recommendation in this report.

The peak demand of 4.8 MW occurred on 22 May 2023 between 14:30 and 15:00 hrs. This is consistent
with the expected summer loading pattern, when the chillers operate at near full capacity to meet the
cooling load of the occupied buildings. The recorded peak is approximately 0.3 MW lower than the
previous year's peak of 5.1 MW, which was recorded in April 2022.

The daily load profile of the facility is characterised by a morning ramp-up starting at
approximately 08:00 hrs, reaching a steady plateau between 10:00 and 12:30 hrs. A second, slightly
higher plateau is observed between 14:00 and 17:00 hrs, coinciding with the afternoon peak in
cooling load and the operation of the cafeteria equipment. The load begins to taper off after 18:00
hrs, with a significant drop after 20:00 hrs when the majority of the IT and office loads are shut
down.

The base load of the facility, observed between 23:00 hrs and 06:00 hrs, is approximately 1.1 MW.
This base load primarily comprises the 24x7 operation of the data centre in Building D, the
security and emergency lighting, and the standby power consumption of the chillers and pumps.

The demand variation between the base load and the peak load is approximately 3.7 MW. This
significant variation presents a clear opportunity for demand-side management, as discussed in
Section 5.4.

According to the Energy Audit Report 2023, GreenScape Tech Park's peak_demand_2023 was 4.8 MW. Record status: current.

**5.3 Demand Contributors**

nature of the operations.

are listed in order of cost-effectiveness and ease of implementation.

**5.4.1 Chiller Sequencing Optimisation (Recommended)**

The existing chiller sequencing logic is based on return water temperature only. It is recommended
to implement a demand-based sequencing algorithm that also considers the outside air temperature and
the building load forecast. This will allow the plant to run one chiller at a higher, more efficient
load factor rather than running both chillers at part load during the shoulder months. The estimated
reduction in peak demand is 0.2 to 0.3 MW. This measure is considered low cost and can be implemented
as part of the existing BMS upgrade.

**5.6 Lighting System Audit**

areas also represent a substantial load, particularly given their long operating hours.

**5.6.2 Lighting Observations and Issues**

The following observations were recorded during the physical verification of the lighting system:

1.  **Magnetic Ballasts:** The FTL fixtures in the common areas of all three buildings are fitted
    with magnetic ballasts. These ballasts are operating at end of their useful life, with several
    exhibiting audible humming and signs of overheating. The efficiency of these ballasts has
    degraded over time, resulting in higher than rated power consumption.
2.  **Inconsistent Occupancy:** The lighting in lobbies, corridors, and staircases is manually
    controlled and remains switched ON for the full duration of the building's operational hours,
    irrespective of occupancy. This is a clear waste of energy, as these areas see very low
    footfall during non-peak hours.
3.  **Car Park Lighting:** The metal halide fixtures in the basement car parks are left ON 24/7.
    While this is partly for security reasons, there is no zoning or dimming strategy in place.
    The lighting level in the car park was measured to be 150 lux, which is significantly higher
    than the recommended 50-75 lux for a car park area.
4.  **Exterior Lighting:** The sodium vapour lamps for the landscape and facade are on a
    time-clock that is set for dusk-to-dawn operation. The clock was found to be correctly set,
    however, there is no astronomical time switch installed, leading to the lights operating for
    longer than necessary during summer months.
5.  **No Central Control:** There is no Building Management System (BMS) integration for the
    lighting circuits. All lighting is controlled via conventional switchboards, making it
    difficult to implement schedules or monitor individual circuit consumption.

documents.title: Energy Audit Report 2023
documents.content:
Key findings indicate that HVAC systems account for the largest share of consumption (48%), followed by lighting (18%) and IT/Data Centre loads (22%). The audit identified 14 improvement opportunities, with a combined potential savings of approximately 1.8 million kWh annually (approx. 14.4% of current consumption). The most significant recommendation is the retrofitting of existing chiller plant controls and the installation of Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) on primary air handling units.

---

**2. FACILITY OVERVIEW**

GreenScape Tech Park (GSTP) is a multi-tenant commercial facility comprising four office blocks (Buildings A, B, C, and D), a central amenities building, two basement levels, and a surface parking area. The total built-up area is 185,000 square meters. The facility operates primarily from 08:00 to 20:00 on weekdays; however, the Data Centre (Building D) and certain critical labs operate 24x7.

The facility receives power from the BESCOM grid at two separate 11 kV feeders. Backup power is provided by four diesel generators (2 x 1250 kVA, 2 x 800 kVA). A 500 kWp rooftop solar PV installation was commissioned in March 2023 and is currently operational.

---

**5. PEAK DEMAND ANALYSIS**

**5.1 Peak Demand Overview**

The maximum demand recorded at the main incoming feeder (11 kV, BESCOM supply) during the
monitoring period was 4.8 MW. According to the Energy Audit Report 2023, GreenScape Tech Park's
peak_demand_2023 was 4.8 MW. This is the current and definitive peak demand value for the facility
for the calendar year 2023, and it has been cross-verified against the 33 kV metering data provided
by BESCOM as well as the internal power quality analyser logs. This value is used as the basis for
all demand-related calculations and recommendation in this report.

The peak demand of 4.8 MW occurred on 22 May 2023 between 14:30 and 15:00 hrs. This is consistent
with the expected summer loading pattern, when the chillers operate at near full capacity to meet the
cooling load of the occupied buildings. The recorded peak is approximately 0.3 MW lower than the
previous year's peak of 5.1 MW, which was recorded in April 2022.

The daily load profile of the facility is characterised by a morning ramp-up starting at
approximately 08:00 hrs, reaching a steady plateau between 10:00 and 12:30 hrs. A second, slightly
higher plateau is observed between 14:00 and 17:00 hrs, coinciding with the afternoon peak in
cooling load and the operation of the cafeteria equipment. The load begins to taper off after 18:00
hrs, with a significant drop after 20:00 hrs when the majority of the IT and office loads are shut
down.

The base load of the facility, observed between 23:00 hrs and 06:00 hrs, is approximately 1.1 MW.
This base load primarily comprises the 24x7 operation of the data centre in Building D, the
security and emergency lighting, and the standby power consumption of the chillers and pumps.

The demand variation between the base load and the peak load is approximately 3.7 MW. This
significant variation presents a clear opportunity for demand-side management, as discussed in
Section 5.4.

According to the Energy Audit Report 2023, GreenScape Tech Park's peak_demand_2023 was 4.8 MW. Record status: current.

**5.3 Demand Contributors**

The key contributors to the peak demand of 4.8 MW are identified as follows:

| Load Group | Estimated Demand at Peak (MW) | Contribution |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| HVAC System (Chillers, Pumps, AHUs) | 2.4 | 50% |
| IT & Data Centre Load (Building D) | 1.3 | 27% |
| Lighting (Common & Tenant Areas) | 0.5 | 10% |
| Lifts & Escalators | 0.3 | 6% |
| Other (Cafeteria, Cafeteria Exhaust, Misc.) | 0.3 | 6% |
| **Total** | **4.8** | **100%** |

The HVAC system is the single largest contributor to the peak demand, as expected. Within the HVAC
system, the two 500 TR centrifugal chillers are the primary drivers. The data centre load in Building
D is the second largest contributor and is considered a non-curtailable load due to the critical
nature of the operations.

**5.4 Demand Reduction Measures**

The following measures have been evaluated to reduce the peak demand of the facility. These measures
are listed in order of cost-effectiveness and ease of implementation.

**5.4.1 Chiller Sequencing Optimisation (Recommended)**

The existing chiller sequencing logic is based on return water temperature only. It is recommended
to implement a demand-based sequencing algorithm that also considers the outside air temperature and
the building load forecast. This will allow the plant to run one chiller at a higher, more efficient
load factor rather than running both chillers at part load during the shoulder months. The estimated
reduction in peak demand is 0.2 to 0.3 MW. This measure is considered low cost and can be implemented
as part of the existing BMS upgrade.

**5.6.2 Lighting Observations and Issues**

The following observations were recorded during the physical verification of the lighting system:

1.  **Magnetic Ballasts:** The FTL fixtures in the common areas of all three buildings are fitted
    with magnetic ballasts. These ballasts are operating at end of their useful life, with several
    exhibiting audible humming and signs of overheating. The efficiency of these ballasts has
    degraded over time, resulting in higher than rated power consumption.
2.  **Inconsistent Occupancy:** The lighting in lobbies, corridors, and staircases is manually
    controlled and remains switched ON for the full duration of the building's operational hours,
    irrespective of occupancy. This is a clear waste of energy, as these areas see very low
    footfall during non-peak hours.
3.  **Car Park Lighting:** The metal halide fixtures in the basement car parks are left ON 24/7.
    While this is partly for security reasons, there is no zoning or dimming strategy in place.
    The lighting level in the car park was measured to be 150 lux, which is significantly higher
    than the recommended 50-75 lux for a car park area.

    time-clock that is set for dusk-to-dawn operation. The clock was found to be correctly set,
    however, there is no astronomical time switch installed, leading to the lights operating for
    longer than necessary during summer months.
5.  **No Central Control:** There is no Building Management System (BMS) integration for the
    lighting circuits. All lighting is controlled via conventional switchboards, making it
    difficult to implement schedules or monitor individual circuit consumption.

**7. Implementation Roadmap and Action Plan**

The recommendations presented in Section 6 and further detailed below require a structured, phased implementation to minimise disruption to building operations and to sequence investments in a manner that yields early savings while de-risking larger capital works. The Facility Management Office (FMO) will act as the nodal agency for coordination, with EcoWatt Solutions providing technical supervision during the first three months of each phase.

**7.1 Phased Implementation Schedule**

The implementation is planned across three phases over a period of 12 to 15 months from the date of approval of this report. Phase I targets quick-win, low-capital measures; Phase II covers mid-cost retrofits; and Phase III involves the major capital projects, including the solar PV installation and the VFD upgrades.

| II | Months 4–9 | Chiller plant optimisation; VFD installation on AHU-12, AHU-14, and pump sets; HVAC duct sealing | 22,00,000 | 14,80,000 | 18 |

It is recommended that all tenders above ₹10,00,000 be processed through the standard two-bid system (technical and financial). For the solar PV installation (Item 8), the evaluation should give weightage to the vendor's track record in similar institutional installations and to the performance guarantee offered. For the chiller replacement (Item 9), the technical bid must require the vendor to provide a detailed energy simulation model in support of the quoted kW/TR.

The FMO notes that the lead time for the water-cooled chillers is approximately 12 weeks from order placement. To avoid slippage in the Phase III timeline, the tender for the chillers should be floated in July 2024, well in advance of the planned replacement date.

**8. Monitoring, Measurement, and Verification (M&V) Plan**

A robust M&V plan is essential to confirm that the anticipated savings are actually realised and to identify any shortfalls early. The following approach, based on the International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol (IPMVP) Option C (whole facility), will be adopted.
